newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea demands France explain Thomson action.
newsitem.headline: South Korea demands France explain Thomson action.

text.p: The South Korean government on Thursday jumped into the controversy over France's suspension of the sale of Thomson SA, saying it was seeking an "understandable explanation" from Paris.
As part of the deal, the sale of Thomson to Lagardere Groupe would have handed consumer electronics giant Thomson Multimedia to South Korea's Daewoo Electronics.
Amid concern in South Korea that racism had blocked the sale, the Seoul foreign ministry said it had issued a cable through its Paris embassy seeking clarification.
"We have requested an understandable explanation from the French government for our public," a foreign ministry official said by telephone.
Seoul wanted to know whether France's Privatisation Commission, which produced a negative report that led to the suspension, "maintained transparency" in its work.
"We would like to know whether the commission's opinion was based on economic factors or public opposition," he said.

French workers took to the streets to demonstrate against selling what they regard as a prize national asset to a foreign company. Thomson labour unions said jobs were at risk, even though Daewoo promised to create 5,000 new jobs.
The French government made clear the decision to put off the sale was because of Daewoo.
"This is a racist decision," said Tony Jung, an electronics analyst at Jardine Fleming Securities.

"The French couldn't accept the fact that Thomson Multimedia was being taken over by a company from a small country in the East. It was hurting their pride. It could have been different if Thomson was taken over by an American company."
South Korean companies in Asia have a reputation for tough, and occasionally brutal, management.
"Day-to-day management would have been a bit more authoritarian than French workers are used to," said Marvin.
Daewoo Electronics Chairman Bae Soon-hoon suggested France was not telling the full story.

"We are trying to find out the real reason behind the French government's announcement of temporarily suspending the privatisation process," a Daewoo spokesman quoted him as saying. "We'll closely examine and confront any development to the situation."
A Daewoo statement said the move was "unexpected and regretful".
The purchase would have transformed struggling Daewoo Electronics into the world's biggest television maker with established brand names and leading edge technology.
"Thomson would have given it a shot at the big league," said Stephen Marvin, head of research at Ssangyong Investment and Securities Co Ltd.
"We've concluded that the deal will take longer than expected, at best, but more likely will be scuttled."

Daewoo is being elbowed aside in its home markets by powerful competitors Samsung Electronics and LG Electronics, and was looking to Thomson to give it a boost with huge economies of scale, brokers said.
Some analysts said the deal never made sense for Daewoo.
"Daewoo is already terribly over-leveraged and losing ground domestically to LG and Samsung," said Matt Cleary, a Seoul-based electronics analyst with HG Asia Ltd.
"I saw this move as one of desperation all along. It just seemed like they had to do something dramatic while they still had the energy to do it."
Analysts said losing the Thomson deal would delay but certainly not halt Daewoo's charge offshore.
"Daewoo will try to take over another high-profile company if the Thomson takeover fails," said Jung of Jardine Fleming.
